q: Logical behaviorism was modeled on Russell and Whitehead's treatment of numbers as:
e: Just as numbers were constructions out of sets, mental events were said to be logical constructions out of actual and possible behavior.

q: What does the logical behaviorist share with the dualist, per Putnam?
a: What goes on in the brain has nothing to do with what we MEAN by 'pain'
w: Belief that pain is a brain state
e: Yet the behaviorist is as 'tough-minded' as the materialist in denying a Cartesian Mind-substance.

q: Putnam famously says of logical behaviorism: 'I come to ______ logical behaviorism, not to ______ it.'
e: He argues that even the weakened forms (analytic entailments, near-translation) are incorrect.

q: Putnam says 'pain' is a cluster-concept. What does he mean?
a: Its application is controlled by a cluster of criteria, all of which are synthetic
w: Pain is just a cluster of behaviors
Pain is defined by one necessary condition
e: The behaviorist would say 'pain stands for a cluster of phenomena'. That is NOT what Putnam means.

q: Putnam's disease analogy (polio, multiple sclerosis) is meant to show that:
a: Causes are not logical constructions out of their effects
e: 'Multiple sclerosis' means the disease normally responsible for certain symptoms, not the symptoms. Likewise pain normally causes pain behavior.

q: Putnam's conclusion about the relation of pains to responses is that pains:
a: Are not clusters of responses, but (normally) the causes of clusters of responses
w: Are identical to clusters of responses
e: This is an empirical fact, and it doesn't rule out worlds where pains produce different responses or none.

a: Feel pain but suppress all involuntary pain behavior
w: Only feel pain in magnetic fields
e: They admit pain only in calm, well-modulated voices. It would be absurd to say they can't feel pain.

a: Suppress even verbal reports of pain and pretend not to know the word
e: If pains were logical constructions out of behavior, X-worlders would behave so as not to have pains. But they do have them.

q: If the X-world story isn't self-contradictory, Putnam says this refutes even logical behaviorism's FIRST (weakest) thesis, which is:
a: There exist analytic entailments between mind-statements and behavior-statements
w: Mental talk is exactly translatable into behavior talk
e: From 'X has a pain' by itself, no behavioral statement follows, not even one with 'normally' or 'probably'.

q: 'Last night at midnight everything doubled in length.' Putnam uses this 'pseudo-hypothesis' to argue that:
a: It actually has testable consequences (e.g., an apparent halving of the speed of light)
e: It's the worst example of an untestable hypothesis. Things in philosophy are rarely as simple as they seem.

q: Why do 'V-waves' that decode into coherent English give better evidence than 'brain spikes'?
a: Spikes could have almost any cause, but coherent language can't arise by chance
e: The 'null hypothesis' of chance can be dismissed, and coherence and simplicity then do real verifying work.

q: Putnam compares inferring X-worlders' pain via theory to inferring what from spectral lines in sunlight?
e: We don't need to heat cadmium on the sun to verify it. Coherence with a vast body of theory is scientific verification.

q: The 'W-waves' (decoded as 'Ho, ho! are we fooling those Earthians!') show that:
a: Even the brain-state = pain principle could reasonably be given up, so it isn't a tautology
e: What's necessarily true is only: an organism in the same state as a human in pain in ALL relevant respects is in pain.

q: Putnam says the logical behaviorist's two escape moves ('change of meaning' and 'untestable') are, respectively:
a: Unreasonable linguistics and unreasonable scientific method
e: They're mutually supporting. 'The circle of reason is to be preferred to any of the many circles of unreason.'

q: In a footnote, Putnam sketches a fourth alternative (beyond dualism, materialism, behaviorism) in which states like pain are defined by:
a: Functional organization, which can be built into many possible physical constitutions
e: This is the seed of functionalism. 'Prefers A to B' doesn't tell us if a creature is carbon, silicon, or even disembodied.
